title: Sylvester Stallone Slams “I Play Rocky” Biopic: “I’m Not Dead Yet—Stop Jumping the Gun!”
body:
Sylvester Stallone, the 78‑year‑old icon behind the “Rocky” and “Rambo” franchises, has publicly weighed in on the upcoming biopic *I Play Rocky*, which dramatizes his rise from a struggling actor to a Hollywood legend. Speaking at a recent event hosted by the nonprofit 92NY, the star praised the film’s lead, Anthony Ippolito, who portrays a young Stallone, and cautioned that the project may be moving ahead faster than the legend himself feels ready for. “I actually thought it was me the first moment I saw him,” Stallone said, adding, “I’m not dead yet. Aren’t we jumping the gun?”

The biopic, slated for a worldwide release later this year, follows the tumultuous journey that culminated in the 1976 release of *Rocky*, a film that not only launched Stallone’s career but also earned the Academy Award for Best Picture. Director Anthony Ippolito, who also co‑writes the screenplay, has been assembling a team of veteran actors and emerging talent to recreate pivotal moments—from the gritty streets of Philadelphia to the high‑stakes negotiations with producers that almost derailed the project. Early screenings at the Toronto International Film Festival have generated buzz, with audiences applauding the film’s reverence for Stallone’s tenacity while also noting its fresh, contemporary storytelling approach.

Stallone’s reaction reflects a broader trend of aging Hollywood figures confronting their own mythologies on screen. In recent years, biopics about living artists—such as *Bohemian Rhapsody* (Freddie Mercury) and *The Eyes of Tammy Faye* (Tammy Faye Bakker)—have sparked debates over artistic license, consent, and the ethics of dramatizing personal histories while the subjects are still alive. Stallone’s comment about “jumping the gun” underscores his awareness of the delicate balance between celebrating his legacy and preserving the authenticity of his lived experience. While he expressed admiration for Ippolito’s performance, the star also hinted at a desire for greater involvement in the narrative, a sentiment echoed by other veterans who have sought creative control over their portrayals.

Industry insiders suggest that Stallone’s endorsement could prove pivotal for the film’s commercial prospects. The actor’s brand remains a powerful draw, and his approval may sway skeptical fans who fear a misrepresentation of the gritty, underdog spirit that defined *Rocky*. Moreover, Stallone’s involvement may open doors for cameo appearances or archival footage that could enrich the storytelling. Yet, the production team has indicated that the script was finalized before Stallone’s formal consultation, a fact that could limit the extent of his influence on the final cut.

Critics who have previewed *I Play Rocky* note that the film attempts to strike a balance between reverent homage and candid examination. Scenes depicting Stallone’s early auditions, the grueling process of writing the *Rocky* screenplay, and the fraught negotiations with United Artists are said to be rendered with a mix of humor and pathos, aiming to humanize the larger‑than‑life persona. The biopic also promises to explore lesser‑known aspects of Stallone’s life, including his struggles with dyslexia, his early financial hardships, and the personal toll of fame. If successful, the film could set a new benchmark for biographical dramas that focus on living subjects, offering a template for collaborative storytelling that respects both artistic vision and personal truth.

As the release date approaches, anticipation builds not only among long‑time fans but also among a new generation discovering Stallone’s legacy through streaming platforms and social media. The film’s performance will likely influence how studios approach future biopics of living icons, potentially prompting more inclusive processes that involve the subjects from script development through post‑production. For Stallone, *I Play Rocky* may serve as both a tribute and a reminder that his story—still unfolding—continues to inspire. Whether the biopic captures the full complexity of his journey remains to be seen, but its very existence signals an enduring fascination with the man who turned a modest boxing drama into a cultural touchstone.
